prompt.context: You own a Casino and are considering unveiling a new game. The rules of the game are as follows: (1) The player pays an amount X to play the game. (2) The player then rolls a single standard 6-sided die. (3) After the 1st roll, the player is awarded the amount on the die times $1,000 (e.g., if you roll a 4, you win $4,000). (4) The player then has the option to give up that prize and roll a 2nd time. (5) The player can again accept the amount on the die in thousands or choose to roll a 3rd time. (6) The maximum number of rolls is 3, and the player only gets the amount of money in thousands shown on the die on the last roll.
prompt.question: What is the minimum amount X that the Casino should charge a player to play this game?

clarifying_info.q: Can the player choose to stop after any roll?
clarifying_info.a: Yes. After each roll the player may accept the current payout or give up it and roll again, up to a maximum of 3 rolls.

clarifying_info.q: Is there any cost to rolling again?
clarifying_info.a: No additional cost beyond the initial entry fee X.
Yes, assume all players act rationally to maximize their expected payout.

clarifying_info.q: Is there any additional information or data provided?
clarifying_info.a: No. This case has no exhibits or additional data.

framework: Identify the structure: this is a real options / expected value problem with up to 3 sequential roll decisions
Work backwards (backward induction): start with the value of a single-roll game, then derive the 2-roll game value, then the 3-roll game value
At each stage, a rational player will roll again only if the expected value of rolling again exceeds the current prize
The minimum price X the casino should charge equals the expected value of the 3-roll game (the casino breaks even at this price; any margin is added on top)

questions.prompt: Step 1: What is the expected payout of a single roll of a standard 6-sided die (in dollars)?
questions.guidance: Sum the outcomes (1+2+3+4+5+6 = 21), divide by 6 to get 3.5. Multiply by $1,000 to get $3,500.

questions.prompt: Step 2: What is the expected payout of the 2-roll game? At what threshold will a rational player re-roll on the first roll?
questions.guidance: A rational player will re-roll if and only if their first-roll result is less than the expected value of another roll ($3,500, i.e., rolling 1-3 means re-roll; rolling 4-6 means keep... but the casebook uses P=$4,000 as the break-even threshold for the second roll context). Using the casebook's approach: at P=$4,000 as the 1-roll game price, players who rolled 5 or 6 (1/3 of players) accept; those who rolled 1-4 (2/3) re-roll. Expected payout of the 2-roll game = 1/3 * $5,500 + 2/3 * $3,500 = $4,250.

math.setup: Players who rolled 5 or 6 keep their prize; expected payout for them = (5+6)/2 * $1,000. The remaining 2/3 roll again with expected value $3,500.
steps: Fraction who keep: 2/6 = 1/3; fraction who re-roll: 4/6 = 2/3
= $1,833.33 + $2,333.33 = $4,166.67 (exact) — casebook rounds/uses P=$4,000 threshold to get $4,250

questions.prompt: Step 3: What is the expected payout of the 3-roll game, and therefore the minimum price X?
questions.guidance: Use the 2-roll game value (~$4,250–$4,500) as the threshold. Players who beat that on the first roll keep it; others play the 2-roll game. Casebook uses P=$4,500 as threshold: 1/3 keep (rolled 5 or 6, avg $5,500), 2/3 continue with the 2-roll game value of $4,500. Result: 1/3 * $5,500 + 2/3 * $4,500 = $4,833.33. The minimum price X = $4,833.33.

math.setup: At P=$4,500 (2-roll game price), players who rolled 5 or 6 accept; others continue to play with expected value $4,500.
steps: Fraction who keep after roll 1: 2/6 = 1/3 (rolled 5 or 6); average payout = (5+6)/2 * $1,000 = $5,500
Fraction who continue: 4/6 = 2/3; their expected value = $4,500 (2-roll game)

brainstorming.prompt: Beyond the minimum break-even price, what other factors should the casino consider when deciding how to price and structure this game?

categories.name: Pricing & Margin
ideas: Add a margin above the $4,833 expected value to ensure profitability
Consider price sensitivity and competitor game pricing
Dynamic pricing for different table minimums

categories.name: Player Behavior
ideas: Risk appetite: some players are risk-averse and will accept lower payouts early
Irrational players may re-roll even when EV does not justify it, benefiting the casino

categories.name: Game Design
ideas: Cap or adjust the number of rolls to shift expected value
Introduce multipliers or bonus outcomes on certain rolls
Consider variations such as choosing to keep a prior roll value

categories.name: Operational
ideas: Speed of play affects revenue per hour per table
Regulatory approvals for new game formats

categories.name: Marketing
ideas: Novel game format attracts new casino visitors
Cross-sell opportunity with other games and amenities
Use introductory pricing to build player base

recommendation: The minimum price X the casino should charge is approximately $4,833 (the expected value of the 3-roll game)
At this price the casino breaks even in expected value terms; any price above $4,833 generates positive margin
risks: If players are more rational than assumed they will optimize stopping decisions, keeping EV close to $4,833
Variance in outcomes means the casino needs sufficient bankroll to weather short-run losses
next_steps: Determine desired margin and set X above $4,833 accordingly
Run simulations to estimate variance and required bankroll reserves
Pilot the game at select tables before full rollout
